bloecke.md:
## The three services of a stock exchange

A stock exchange does not hold any securities of its own for sale. It provides three separate services that you should keep apart, because different trading venues provide them to different standards.

The first service is **price discovery**. Thousands of individual intentions to buy and sell produce a single price that everyone can see. The second is the provision of **liquidity**. An investor who wants to sell does not have to look for a buyer, because one can be found in the system at every second of trading hours. The third is securing **settlement**. Once a trade has been concluded, a central counterparty steps in between buyer and seller, so that neither side has to rely on the unknown party on the other side delivering and paying.

The third service is the least visible. In the EU, securities transactions are settled two business days after the trade, T+2 for short. The USA, Canada and Mexico switched to T+1 in May 2024, and the EU has agreed on 11 October 2027 as the date for the changeover. Between trade and delivery there is therefore a period in which someone bears the default risk of the other side. Clearing exists for this purpose. That is why the position appears in the portfolio immediately after the purchase, while the money is only finally booked later.

bloecke.md:
## Primary market and secondary market

A company receives money from its securities only once, namely when they are issued. Investors who subscribe for a share in an IPO or buy a newly issued bond are financing the issuer. This part of the market is called the **primary market**. All subsequent trading takes place on the **secondary market**. There the securities merely change hands between investors, and the issuer receives no money from these transactions.

The secondary market still matters to the issuer, because it determines the price at which the next issue can be placed. The German federal government issues its securities through auctions to a fixed group of bidders. These include Bubills with maturities of up to twelve months, Treasury notes (Schätze) with two years, Bobls with five and German federal bonds (Bundesanleihen) with seven to thirty years. The yield the federal government has to offer depends on the secondary market on the day of the auction. The same applies to every company planning a capital increase.

The secondary market brings the issuer no money. It does, however, determine the price at which the issuer raises money in its next issue, and it gives investors the certainty that they can sell their securities again. Together, these two points are the reason investors are willing to subscribe on the primary market.

## The order book

A traditional stock exchange is built on a sorted list. The **bid side** shows all buy orders with a limit, in descending order of price, and the **ask side** all sell orders, in ascending order. Within a price level, the order of arrival decides (price-time priority). As long as the best bid and the best ask do not cross, no trade takes place. Only an order that accepts a price on the other side triggers a trade. The price of the last trade is the price that apps and newspapers display.

The gap between the best bid and the best ask is called the [[Bid-ask spread|bid-ask spread]]. It is the price of being able to trade immediately. You pay it whenever you buy or sell immediately. Investors who can wait may earn it themselves by placing a limit order in the book and waiting for execution.

Deutsche Börse's investor portal shows the ten best price levels per side for Xetra, with the volume at each level. Professional market data contains the entire visible book down to the individual order. What remains hidden are mainly portions of large orders that appear in the book only piece by piece as iceberg orders. The displayed spread is therefore only part of the information. The other part is the depth of the book, that is, how many units are available at each price level.

A buy order without a limit for 1,500 units meets the order book above. It is executed on the ask side from the bottom up: first the 400 units at 48.01, then the 600 at 48.02, then 500 of the 800 units at 48.04.

The total cost is €72,036, and the average price is €48.024. That is €21 more than at the best ask of 48.01 and €28.50 more than at the mid price of 48.005. These extra costs do not appear on any fee statement, because they are included in the execution price.

bloecke.md:
## Market makers and quoting

Outside Xetra, prices are formed differently. On gettex, Baader Bank provides the prices for shares, ETFs, funds and bonds, and on LS Exchange, Lang & Schwarz is the sole market maker. There is no book with many competing limits there. Instead, a single firm quotes the bid and ask prices and trades against its own inventory, which is known as quoting. Both venues charge no brokerage fee (Courtage) and no exchange fee; the market maker earns from the spread. This is not meant as a criticism. It describes how a trading venue that costs the investor nothing makes its living.

Xetra has such commitments too. For thinly traded securities, designated sponsors undertake to provide binding bid and ask prices. The difference lies in competition. Where several market makers and many investors are quoting at the same time, the spread is narrow. Where only one market maker is quoting and the reference market has closed, the market maker prices in its own risk.

Not every market is an exchange market. Bonds other than the large government bonds are traded largely through dealer networks and not through a visible order book. An investor who buys a position there via a trading venue is in practice dealing with a single firm.

bloecke.md:
## Auctions

A trading day on Xetra begins with an **opening auction** at 9:00, and only after that does continuous trading start. In the auction, all orders received are collected. The price is determined according to the maximum executable volume principle, that is, so that the largest volume is traded. An intraday auction follows in the course of the day. After continuous trading ends at 17:30, the **closing auction** takes place. It ends at a random moment so that nobody can deliberately exploit the last second. For securities in the DAX, MDAX and SDAX, trading at the determined closing auction price is then still possible for five minutes.

Unlike in continuous trading, all participants in an auction get the same price. A buyer with a limit of 48.20 therefore pays 48.05 if the auction price is 48.05. The limit is an upper bound and not a price offer.

If a potential price leaves the dynamic corridor around the last price or the static corridor around the last auction price, Xetra suspends trading for at least 120 seconds and reopens it via an auction. For ETFs, ETCs and ETNs there is a tiered model for this, with corridors that widen step by step. Since the flash crash of 6 May 2010, the US exchanges have had comparable circuit breakers. On that day the S&P 500 fell by a further 5% to 6% within about four minutes.

Getting an obviously wrong price cancelled after the event, on the other hand, is difficult. On the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, a mistrade in Xetra transactions must be applied for within 30 minutes of receipt of the trade confirmation, and in specialist trading on Börse Frankfurt within two trading hours. In addition, a share transaction on Xetra is only cancelled if its price deviates from the fair market price by at least 5% and by at least €0.50.

## Trading hours and exchange holidays

The major stock markets are never all open at the same time, and this affects prices more than most investors assume. Tokyo closes early in the German morning, London trades largely in parallel with Frankfurt, and the US exchanges only open at 9:30 New York time, which is 15:30 German time. Between 15:30 and 17:30, Europe and the USA are open at the same time. During this period, liquidity is highest for all globally traded securities.

This has a consequence that is easily overlooked but costs money. At the end of August 2026, a world ETF on the MSCI World contained around 72% US shares. If you buy it at 9:05, these 72% have not been traded since the previous evening. The market maker estimates their value and gets paid for the uncertainty through a wider spread. In the afternoon, when the underlying shares themselves are being traded, it can hedge at any time and quotes correspondingly tighter prices.

In addition, exchange holidays differ from public holidays. In 2026, Xetra is closed on 1 January, 3 and 6 April, 1 May and 24, 25 and 31 December. Trading does take place, however, on Ascension Day, Whit Monday and Corpus Christi.

- Trade during Xetra core hours, and for globally diversified products preferably in the afternoon. In off-peak hours, the extra costs arise through the spread and not through fees.
- Before execution, compare the price on your trading venue with the Xetra price. If it differs noticeably without any current news, the timing is poorly chosen.
- For every free trading venue, check how it makes its money. It is almost always the spread.

mitnehmen: A stock exchange provides price discovery, liquidity and secure settlement, and different trading venues deliver these three services to different standards.
The displayed price is the last price paid; the tradable prices are the bid and ask, and you pay the spread between them on every immediate trade.
Larger orders run through several price levels of the order book, so their average price is worse than the best ask without any fee showing it.
In an auction everyone gets the same price, in continuous trading price-time priority applies, and a limit is only a price boundary.
Long trading hours outside Xetra have a drawback, because there a single market maker often quotes without an open reference market.

begriffe.text: Sorted list of all limit buy and sell orders for a security on a trading venue. In continuous trading, price-time priority applies. The better price takes precedence, and at the same price the earlier order.
Difference between the highest bid to buy (bid) and the lowest offer to sell (ask). It is the price of being able to trade immediately and widens when trading is thin and outside core trading hours.
Trading firm that provides binding bid and ask prices and trades against its own inventory. On trading venues without a brokerage fee, it earns from the spread instead of a fee.
Trading in securities that have already been issued, between investors. The issuer receives no money from it, but its cost of financing depends on the price level on the secondary market.
Temporary suspension of continuous trading when a potential price leaves a predefined corridor. Trading then resumes via an auction.
